segments.title: Joséphine and the dispersal of Malmaison
segments.text:
Stop outside number sixteen.

Today, passers-by see just another address in the Opéra district.

But in March eighteen nineteen, this place brought several worlds together: the vanished French Empire, the world of science, faraway voyages and the collectors of Paris.

There was an auction here.

And the objects offered for sale came from Malmaison.

To understand how they arrived in this street, we need to meet the woman who had brought them together.

Joséphine de Beauharnais.

She had shared the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte, become Empress of the French, and then been divorced when Napoleon sought to secure the imperial succession.

Yet the Château de Malmaison, near Paris, remained her own particular world.

It was much more than an elegant home.

Over the years, she had turned it into a meeting place for gardens, works of art, curiosities, plants and rare animals.

Joséphine had a particular passion for botany.

She supported horticultural projects and collected plants brought from distant parts of the world.

In an age of major scientific expeditions, owning an unfamiliar plant or an object brought back from a voyage could reveal several things at once: a collector's curiosity, the ambitions of the state, and the networks of power that made such acquisitions possible.

But Joséphine died on the twenty-ninth of May, eighteen fourteen, shortly after Napoleon's first abdication.

She would never see his brief return to power in eighteen fifteen, or the Empire's second fall.

France changed its government.

Properties changed hands.

But fortunes, and debts, did not simply disappear.

Her son, Eugène de Beauharnais, inherited a substantial part of his mother's property.

There were financial obligations to settle as part of the estate.

And some of the collections were put up for sale.

This is where our little Parisian street enters the story.

The catalogue announced an auction originally due to begin on the fifteenth of March, eighteen nineteen.

It was postponed to the twenty-fourth.

And before the auctioneer's hammer began to fall, there were to be days when prospective buyers could inspect the objects.

Imagine the scene.

There's no need to invent the actions of any particular visitor.

People enter to examine the lots.

Some recognise the artists' names.

Others assess the material, the rarity, or the provenance of an object.

A dealer might consider its resale value.

A collector of curiosities might be drawn to something unusual.

Another visitor might want a souvenir of Malmaison.

The same object could mean entirely different things to different people.

Now, let's open the catalogue.

This isn't an ordinary household furniture sale.

There are sculptures and statues.

Vases. Tables. Marble objects. Engraved stones. Mosaics. Decorative pieces.

And then, gradually, the list takes a rather unexpected turn.

Minerals.

Shells.

Preserved birds.

Weapons and clothing from regions far beyond Europe.

And even objects described as mummies.

Mummies.

Offered at an auction on Rue Louis-le-Grand, in the spring of eighteen nineteen.

That word makes us stop and think today.

In historical classifications, it could refer to human remains. And that immediately raises questions about provenance, and about the treatment of the dead.

But nineteenth-century catalogues don't always tell us everything we would like to know.

Where, exactly, did these objects come from?

Who collected them?

Under what circumstances?

Through whose hands did they pass before reaching Malmaison?

An auction catalogue describes what is for sale.

It does not necessarily reconstruct an object's entire history.

That distinction is essential.

Some of these curiosities point towards the great era of European exploration in the early nineteenth century.

The catalogue connects certain pieces with the expedition led by the navigator Nicolas Baudin, who set out for southern waters in the early eighteen hundreds.

That scientific undertaking explored parts of the Australian coastline and brought many observations and collections back to Europe.

For Joséphine, the connections between major expeditions, scientists and the collections at Malmaison were particularly important.

But we cannot simply assign every item in the catalogue to a particular ship, collector or port of call.

The history of an object depends on evidence of its provenance.

Even so, think about the possible journey of some of these pieces.

From a coastline on the other side of the world.

Onto a ship, and then into a French port.

From a scientific collection into the rooms of Malmaison.

And, years later, to number sixteen, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Something that may once have represented an extraordinary discovery becomes a numbered auction lot.

It is examined.

Valued.

Sold.

And carried away to another collection.

The sale also brought several periods of history together.

Among the objects were works and sculptures associated with the court of Louis the Sixteenth.

Some were linked to the Queen's Dairy at Rambouillet, a decorative complex created in the world of Marie Antoinette.

What a remarkable meeting of destinies.

Objects from a royal court overturned by the Revolution.

The collection of Joséphine, a former empress.

And then an auction in eighteen nineteen, under the restored monarchy.

In only a few decades, political power had changed hands again and again.

But objects could survive the fall of regimes.

Perhaps that's what makes this story so unusual.

At Malmaison, the collections had formed a whole.

There were books, gardens, a cabinet of curiosities, ceremonial rooms and personal souvenirs.

Together, they reflected the taste of a woman, her position in society and the age in which she lived.

But an auction breaks up that unity.

Things assembled over many years can be scattered in just a few sale sessions.

One sculpture goes to a house.

A vase is bought by an enthusiast.

A scientific curiosity passes into someone else's collection.

Sometimes an object's later journey can be traced through inventories, annotated catalogues and museum archives.

Others become difficult to follow.

The catalogue of eighteen nineteen is rather like a snapshot of a world at the precise moment it comes apart.

Look again at number sixteen.

The façade you can see today is later than the auction. It would be wrong to pretend we can identify the actual room where the sale took place.

But the address allows us to place the episode in the city.

Here, for a few days, the collections of Malmaison met the dealers and collectors of Paris.

We could tell Joséphine's story entirely through palaces, portraits and the grand ceremonies of the Empire.

But this place gives us another way to meet her.

Through the things left behind after her death.

Through the objects her heirs had to part with.

And through the traces preserved in old catalogues.

On one side, a woman who had sought to bring together the beauties and curiosities of the world.

On the other, an auction room where that collection becomes a succession of separate lots.

And between the two, only five years since her death.

A life doesn't disappear entirely when a person dies.

Books, furniture and treasured objects continue to travel.

But once separated, they no longer tell quite the same story.

It's time to leave this address.

Our next stop will take us to a building every bit as famous as Malmaison, but we'll see it under radically different circumstances.

The Palais Garnier.

And Paris, in August nineteen forty-four.
